apiVersion: v1

  labels:
    project: chaos-eater

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: carts
  labels:
    name: carts
    project: chaos-eater
  namespace: sock-shop
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      name: carts
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        name: carts
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: carts
        image: weaveworksdemos/carts:0.4.8
        env:
        - name: JAVA_OPTS
          value: -Xms64m -Xmx128m -XX:+UseG1GC -Djava.security.egd=file:/dev/urandom
            -Dspring.zipkin.enabled=false
        resources:
          limits:
            memory: 512Mi
            cpu: 1000m
          requests:
            cpu: 100m
            memory: 200Mi
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        securityContext:
          runAsNonRoot: true
          runAsUser: 10001
          capabilities:
            drop:
            - all
            add:
            - NET_BIND_SERVICE
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
        volumeMounts:
        - mountPath: /tmp
          name: tmp-volume
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
      volumes:
      - name: tmp-volume
        emptyDir:
          medium: Memory
      nodeSelector:
        beta.kubernetes.io/os: linux

Issue #0: Single replica points of failure

- details: All deployments run exactly one replica. If the pod is killed, crashes, or its node fails, the service has no redundant instance to handle traffic, resulting in downtime until a replacement is scheduled. For stateful components, a single replica also puts data at risk if the pod is rescheduled.
- manifests having the issues: ['sock-shop-2/manifests/01-carts-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/03-carts-db-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/05-catalogue-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/07-catalogue-db-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/09-front-end-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/11-orders-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/13-orders-db-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/15-payment-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/17-queue-master-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/19-rabbitmq-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/21-session-db-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/23-shipping-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/25-user-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/27-user-db-dep.yaml']
- problematic config: replicas: 1 in all Deployment specs

Issue #1: No persistent storage for stateful services

- details: Database and message broker deployments (carts-db, catalogue-db, orders-db, rabbitmq, session-db, user-db) do not use PersistentVolumeClaims. Their data is stored in the ephemeral container filesystem. On pod deletion, node failure, or rescheduling, the data is lost, causing service unavailability and inconsistency.
- manifests having the issues: ['sock-shop-2/manifests/03-carts-db-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/07-catalogue-db-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/13-orders-db-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/19-rabbitmq-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/21-session-db-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/27-user-db-dep.yaml']
- problematic config: No persistent volume claim; no volume mounted to the data directory (e.g., /data/db, /var/lib/mysql, /var/lib/rabbitmq, /data)

Issue #2: Read-only root filesystem without writable data volume

- details: Stateful containers set `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` but do not mount a writable volume at their data directory. This prevents the application from writing data and can cause immediate crash loops or inability to start. For mongo, directory /data/db; for rabbitmq, /var/lib/rabbitmq; for redis, /data. This is a fatal misconfiguration that becomes evident during any pod restart or failover.
- manifests having the issues: ['sock-shop-2/manifests/03-carts-db-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/13-orders-db-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/19-rabbitmq-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/21-session-db-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/27-user-db-dep.yaml']
- problematic config: securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem: true without a writable volume mount for the application's data directory

Issue #3: Missing liveness and readiness probes

- details: Several deployments do not define liveness or readiness probes. If a container becomes unresponsive (e.g., due to deadlock, OOM, heavy load) but the process remains alive, Kubernetes continues to send traffic to the pod, causing failed requests. Readiness probes are also necessary to avoid routing traffic to pods that are still starting up. During failure injection, this can amplify outages.
- manifests having the issues: ['sock-shop-2/manifests/01-carts-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/03-carts-db-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/07-catalogue-db-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/11-orders-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/13-orders-db-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/17-queue-master-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/19-rabbitmq-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/21-session-db-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/23-shipping-dep.yaml', 'sock-shop-2/manifests/27-user-db-dep.yaml']
- problematic config: Absence of livenessProbe and readinessProbe in container spec

Issue #4: Sidecar container failure restarts entire pod

- details: In rabbitmq deployment, the pod contains a sidecar (rabbitmq-exporter) alongside the main rabbitmq container. If the sidecar exits or fails, the pod restarts (default restartPolicy: Always), causing downtime for the rabbitmq message broker and potentially losing in-memory messages or connections.

elems.description: The most glaring issue is that every deployment runs a single replica, creating a single point of failure. I selected the front-end deployment because it is the sole entry point to the Sock Shop application; if its only pod becomes unavailable, the entire store is inaccessible from outside. The steady state that reflects normal operation is that the front-end deployment has exactly 1 available replica, meaning the pod is ready and serving traffic. This is easily measured via the deployment's status.availableReplicas field and is directly disrupted by pod deletion, node failure, or container crashes, making it the easiest issue to verify with chaos engineering.

from kubernetes import client, config

def main():

    if os.getenv("KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST"):

    v1 = client.AppsV1Api()
    namespace = "sock-shop"

    available_replicas_list = []
    for i in range(args.duration):
        try:

            available = dep.status.available_replicas or 0
            available_replicas_list.append(available)
            print("Time {}: availableReplicas={}".format(i+1, available))

    print("Summary over {} seconds: ".format(args.duration))

    if all(x == 1 for x in available_replicas_list):

class SteadyStateTest(K8sAPIBase):
    def test_frontend_available_replicas(self, duration):
        # Create an AppsV1Api client using the same configuration loaded in K8sAPIBase.
        apps_v1 = client.AppsV1Api()
        namespace = "sock-shop"
        name = "front-end"

        observations = []  # Boolean list: True if availableReplicas >= 1
        consecutive_zeros = 0  # Current streak of observations with 0 available replicas
        max_consecutive_zeros = 0  # Maximum streak observed

        for i in range(duration):
            try:
                # Read the deployment's status to get available replicas.
                dep = apps_v1.read_namespaced_deployment(name=name, namespace=namespace)
                available = dep.status.available_replicas or 0
                ok = available >= 1
            except Exception as e:
                # On error, treat as unavailable (availableReplicas = 0) to be conservative.
                print("Error at time {}: {}".format(i + 1, e))
                available = 0
                ok = False

            observations.append(ok)

            # Update consecutive zero tracking.
            if ok:
                consecutive_zeros = 0
            else:
                consecutive_zeros += 1
                max_consecutive_zeros = max(max_consecutive_zeros, consecutive_zeros)

            print("Time {}: availableReplicas={} -> {}".format(i + 1, available, "OK" if ok else "NOT OK"))

            if i < duration - 1:
                time.sleep(1)

        total = len(observations)
        good = sum(observations)
        availability_ratio = good / total if total > 0 else 0

        # Threshold checks:
        # 1. availableReplicas >= 1 for at least 99% of the observations.
        meets_ratio = availability_ratio >= 0.99
        # 2. No dip to 0 lasting more than 1 consecutive second.
        meets_zero_tolerance = max_consecutive_zeros <= 1

        # Summary output for both success and failure cases.
        print()
        print("Summary over {} seconds:".format(duration))
        print("Total observations: {}".format(total))
        print("Observations with availableReplicas >= 1: {} ({:.2f}%)".format(good, availability_ratio * 100))
        print("Max consecutive zeros: {}".format(max_consecutive_zeros))
        print("Availability ratio threshold (>=99%): {}".format("PASS" if meets_ratio else "FAIL"))
        print("Consecutive zero threshold (<=1): {}".format("PASS" if meets_zero_tolerance else "FAIL"))

        # Assert both conditions to verify the steady state.
        assert meets_ratio, "Availability ratio {:.2f}% is below 99% threshold".format(availability_ratio * 100)
        assert meets_zero_tolerance, "Max consecutive zeros {} exceeds 1 second".format(max_consecutive_zeros)
        print("Steady-state threshold satisfied.")


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--duration", type=int, default=5, help="Duration in seconds")
    args = parser.parse_args()

fault.description: The Sock Shop microservices are all single-replica deployments, so each component is a single point of failure. Next, NetworkChaos injects packet loss/partition on the same pods to mimic a DDoS attack, which can cause liveness/readiness failures and force restarts. Then PodChaos pod-kill on front-end and carts-db simulates attackers deliberately killing critical pods, which is maximally impactful because there are no redundant replicas, and the carts-db restart reveals the read-only filesystem/persistence flaw that prevents recovery. Finally, PodChaos container-kill on the rabbitmq-exporter sidecar simulates a sidecar crash, which restarts the whole rabbitmq pod due to shared process group, disrupting order/queue processing. This sequence reveals the vulnerabilities of single replicas, storage misconfiguration, missing probes, and sidecar-caused pod restarts.

time_schedule.thought: The experiment must validate the two steady states before, during, and after fault injection. Pre-validation needs enough time to establish a reliable baseline; I allocate 2 minutes to collect ~120 observations per steady state, which is sufficient to confirm the 99% and 95% availability thresholds with high confidence. Fault injection should cover all four fault groups in the described sequence: StressChaos on front-end and carts-db, NetworkChaos (packet loss) on the same services, PodChaos pod-kill targeting front-end and carts-db, and finally PodChaos container-kill on the rabbitmq-exporter sidecar. I allocate 6 minutes for fault injection: 1.5 minutes for StressChaos, 1.5 minutes for NetworkChaos, 2 minutes for PodChaos pod-kill (to observe potential crash-loops and recovery attempts), and 1 minute for the container-kill sidecar failure. This provides enough observation windows to detect steady-state violations. Post-validation runs for 2 minutes to verify that both deployments return to their expected available replica counts after the faults are withdrawn. The total time is the sum of 2m + 6m + 2m = 10m.

pre_validation.thought: In the pre-validation phase, both steady-state unit tests are scheduled to run concurrently from the very start of the phase (grace_period=0s) and continue for the entire 2-minute duration. This approach ensures that the front-end deployment and the carts-db deployment are observed simultaneously over a long period, confirming that the system is fully stable and meeting the availability thresholds before any faults are injected. Running them in parallel is particularly important because these services are part of the same microservices application and may affect each other's availability; observing both at the same time guarantees that the steady-state conditions hold for the whole system. The full 2-minute duration is used to maximize the confidence in the pre-injection state and to detect any subtle transient issues that might otherwise go unnoticed in a shorter observation window.

fault_injection.thought: The fault-injection phase lasts 6 minutes. I divided the 6-minute window into four sequential fault blocks to mirror the described Black Friday attack sequence: (1) StressChaos on front-end and carts-db for the first 1m30s to simulate heavy load; (2) NetworkChaos packet loss on the same pods for the next 1m30s to simulate DDoS; (3) PodChaos pod-kill on front-end and carts-db for 1m30s to simulate targeted pod destruction; and (4) PodChaos container-kill on the rabbitmq-exporter sidecar for the final 1m30s to simulate a sidecar crash that restarts the rabbitmq pod. Each group starts precisely when the previous group ends, so the fault injections are sequential. Within each group, faults targeting different pods run simultaneously. I run both steady-state unit tests (frontendDeploymentAvailableReplicas and cartsDbDeploymentAvailableReplicas) continuously for the entire 6-minute phase, sampling every second, so that unavailability caused by any fault is captured. This continuous monitoring also ensures we observe the transition between fault periods and can detect if a steady-state violation persists beyond the fault window.

post_validation.thought: In the post-validation phase, after the fault injection phase concludes, I allow a 30-second grace period for the system to stabilize: any pods killed or restarted by the chaos experiments should have been rescheduled and become ready, and the effects of stress and network loss should have dissipated. I then launch two steady-state verification tests concurrently: one for frontendDeploymentAvailableReplicas and one for cartsDbDeploymentAvailableReplicas. They run for 60 seconds, sampling the deployment status every second, which provides 60 observations per test. This is sufficient to statistically validate the 99%/95% availability thresholds. Running them in parallel is safe because they are read-only Kubernetes API queries and do not interfere with each other or with the system under test. The total elapsed time is 90 seconds, leaving 30 seconds of buffer within the 2-minute phase.

plan.summary: The chaos engineering experiment spans a total of 10 minutes, divided into three phases: pre-validation (2 minutes), fault injection (6 minutes), and post-validation (2 minutes). During the pre-validation phase, both steady-state verification workflows, frontendDeploymentAvailableReplicas and cartsDbDeploymentAvailableReplicas, run concurrently from the very beginning with a grace period of 0 seconds and a duration of exactly 2 minutes, allowing the system to be observed for 120 seconds per test to establish a reliable baseline and confirm availability thresholds before any faults are introduced. The fault-injection phase lasts 6 minutes and is organized into four sequential fault blocks, each starting immediately when the previous one ends, with the two steady-state verification workflows continuing to run concurrently for the entire 6-minute duration, sampling every second to capture any availability violations. The first fault block begins at time 0 seconds and runs for 1 minute 30 seconds, injecting StressChaos simultaneously on the front-end and carts-db services (two separate StressChaos fault injections, both with grace period 0 seconds and duration 1 minute 30 seconds). The second fault block starts at exactly 1 minute 30 seconds and also lasts 1 minute 30 seconds, injecting NetworkChaos (packet loss) concurrently on the same two services (two NetworkChaos fault injections, both with grace period 1 minute 30 seconds and duration 1 minute 30 seconds). The third fault block starts at 3 minutes and runs for 1 minute 30 seconds, injecting PodChaos pod-kill faults concurrently on front-end and carts-db (two PodChaos fault injections, both with grace period 3 minutes and duration 1 minute 30 seconds). The fourth and final fault block starts at 4 minutes 30 seconds and runs for 1 minute 30 seconds, injecting a PodChaos container-kill fault targeting the rabbitmq-exporter sidecar (one PodChaos fault injection with grace period 4 minutes 30 seconds and duration 1 minute 30 seconds), simulating a sidecar crash that restarts the rabbitmq pod. Throughout the entire 6-minute fault-injection phase, both steady-state checks run without interruption, ensuring continuous monitoring across fault transitions. The post-validation phase begins after the fault injection phase ends, with a 30-second grace period to allow the system to stabilize; after this grace period, at 30 seconds into the phase, both frontendDeploymentAvailableReplicas and cartsDbDeploymentAvailableReplicas steady-state verification workflows are launched concurrently and run for 60 seconds, providing 60 observations per test to statistically confirm that the deployments have returned to their expected available replica counts. This leaves a 30-second buffer at the end of the 2-minute phase. Overall, the experiment ensures that steady-state conditions are validated before, during, and after each fault injection, with precise timings for every action.

analysis_history.report:
The fault-injection phase failed to maintain the frontendDeploymentAvailableReplicas steady state. The measured availability was 91.11%, below the required 99% threshold, meaning that for approximately 8.9% of the 360-second fault-injection period (about 32 one-second observations) the front-end Deployment had zero available replicas. This directly violates the steady-state assertion and disproves the hypothesis that the system remains stable under the injected faults.

Root causes are directly tied to the front-end Deployment configuration and the fault sequence. The front-end Deployment (sock-shop-2/manifests/09-front-end-dep.yaml) runs exactly 1 replica (spec.replicas: 1). This makes the front-end pod a single point of failure: whenever that pod is killed, unhealthy, or not ready, there are no other pods to serve traffic, and availableReplicas drops to 0. The fault scenario deliberately targeted this single pod with three consecutive fault blocks: (1) StressChaos injecting 100% CPU load and 256MB memory stress; (2) NetworkChaos injecting 50% packet loss “to” the front-end pod; (3) PodChaos pod-kill on the front-end pod. The front-end container has resource limits of cpu: 1000m and memory: 512Mi, and it runs a web server on port 8079. Under CPU/memory stress, the existing readiness and liveness probes (httpGet on /, port 8079) can time out or fail, causing Kubernetes to mark the pod as unready or restart it. Under 50% packet loss, probes from the kubelet can also fail intermittently, leading to repeated unavailability and restarts. Most decisively, the pod-kill fault removes the only front-end replica. After a kill, Kubernetes must schedule and start a new pod, and the readiness probe has initialDelaySeconds: 30, so the replacement pod is not considered available for at least 30 seconds (plus container startup/image-pull time). Thus a single pod-kill alone can produce a 30-60 second outage, which in a 360-second observation window corresponds to ~8-16% unavailability—enough to fail the 99% requirement. The observed ~32 zero-value seconds are consistent with a combination of stress-induced probe failures, network-loss-induced restarts, and the pod-kill recovery delay.

Additionally, the steady-state threshold also requires no consecutive zero observations longer than 1 second; a pod-kill recovery inherently takes many seconds, so this condition was certainly violated as well, even though the script reported the ratio assertion first.

To improve resiliency and prevent this failure, the following changes are recommended:
- Increase the replica count for the front-end Deployment to at least 2 (ideally 3) so that the service remains available during a pod kill or node failure. The Service selector only matches the front-end pod label, and with multiple replicas the Service will send traffic to the healthy ones.
- Add a PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) for the front-end Deployment to guarantee a minimum number of available replicas during voluntary disruptions.
- Consider configuring anti-affinity or pod distribution constraints so that replicas are spread across different nodes, protecting against node-level failures.
- For stress/load resilience, configure a HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA) based on CPU/memory usage so the deployment can scale out before becoming saturated.
- Review and tune the readiness and liveness probe settings (e.g., timeoutSeconds, periodSeconds, failureThreshold) so transient CPU spikes or packet loss do not cause the sole replica to be marked unready unnecessarily; however, with multiple replicas, even if one pod is temporarily unready the steady-state availability is maintained.
- The front-end container should not be a single point of failure; the above scaling and distribution changes directly address the observed failure and are sufficient to pass the steady-state threshold under the given fault scenario.
